title: M/S Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors. (with connected appeals)
neutral_citation: Civil Appeal Nos. 3607-3610 of 2008, with C.A. Nos. 4104-4107 of 2008
coram: Ajay Rastogi & B.V. Nagarathna, JJ. (delivered by Nagarathna, J.)
docket: Civil Appeal Nos. 3607-3610 of 2008 (with C.A. Nos. 4104-4107 of 2008)
disposition: Appeals allowed; Appellate Tribunal's order cancelling JSPL's distribution licence set aside (licence restored)
headnote: Not a Supply Code case in substance — this is a landmark ruling on the DISTRIBUTION-LICENSING scheme under Sections 9, 10, 14, 15, 19 and 42(2) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (grant/cancellation of a distribution licence to a captive-power-plant owner supplying a private industrial estate, the 'minimum area of supply' Explanation to Rule 3 of the 2005 Distribution Rules, and natural justice before a Section 142 penalty), rather than the consumer-facing billing/assessment/disconnection/security provisions that are the focus of this Supply Code jurisprudence project. Recorded here only for completeness of the source corpus; flagged OFFTOPIC to the provision index (though the general Electricity Act framework it construes forms useful background).

holding_units.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.9, 10, 14, 15, 19, 42(2)) and Distribution of Electricity (Additional Requirement of Capital Adequacy...) Rules, 2005
holding_units.clause: ss.9/10 (captive plant vs generating company); Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply); s.19 (revocation); s.142 (penalty/natural justice)
holding_units.topic: Distribution licence grant/cancellation; minimum-area Explanation is a guideline, not a rigid bar, on these unusual facts; penalty requires a hearing
holding_units.holding: The Supreme Court restored a distribution licence earlier granted to JSPL (a captive-power-plant owner, governed by s.9 not s.10 of the Act) to supply a private industrial estate it had itself developed under a State Government MoU/permission predating the 2003 Act's full commencement and the 2005 Rules. The Appellate Tribunal had wrongly treated the Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply = a municipal area or revenue district) as an inflexible bar to a second/parallel licence in a smaller area; the Court held the historical background — investment made, the State's own power shortage, CSEB's admitted inability to supply the area, and long-term supply contracts already in place before the Rules existed — justified treating the case as an exception, and estoppel/vested-rights principles militated against retrospectively invalidating the licence. Separately, the Commission's Rs. 1 lakh penalty under s.142 for supplying without a licence was rightly set aside by the Tribunal for want of a hearing, since the licensing proceeding itself never framed the question of JSPL's liability to penalty.
holding_units.limiting_facts: JSPL, a captive power plant, supplied electricity from 1.3.2004 to industries in a private industrial estate it had developed with State Government concurrence predating the 2003 Act's full force; the State Electricity Regulatory Commission granted it a distribution licence in 2005 for two villages, which the Appellate Tribunal cancelled in 2008 (applying the 'minimum area' Explanation to Rule 3), disrupting supply to ~30 industries and ~4000 employees.
holding_units.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~57 pages) and its subject (distribution licensing, not Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection); not exhaustively digested. General electricity-law background only.
